#649. Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

The human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

That would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

However, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Each new fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle said.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record."

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

An important concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

This approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

Together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

As a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species currently classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

The idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

Such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever new fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

The proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as new evidence has accumulated.

"The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle said.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups."

Ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.

#647. ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Names Historic Season 35 Winner: See All the Scores, Who Won

Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood competed for their chance to win the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

[This story contains spoilers for the season finale of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]

Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is officially over, and the show has crowned a new winner.

The finale episode of DWTS saw couples compete in three rounds of competition as Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood battled it out for a chance to win the season 35 Len Goodman mirrorball trophy.

Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach were ultimately named the winner’s of DWTS season 35; his win makes him the first amputee winner of the series. Related Stories TV Where to Stream 'Dancing With the Stars' Season 35 Finale Live Online 'Dancing' Diaries Alfonso Ribeiro on the "Wild" Ride of 'DWTS' Season 35, Reuniting With Tatyana Ali and Why He Won't Compete in an All-Winners Season

The Paralympian previously told The Hollywood Reporter it would be “very, very special” to become the first amputee winner of DWTS. “Of course, getting the opportunity to make the finale, to win the show, to get to represent the disabled community in that way and become the first amputee to win Dancing With the Stars would be very, very special, and would mean a lot to myself and hopefully to all people with disabilities and the community as a whole,” he said.

Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov placed second. Maura and Mark Ballas came in fifth, with Tatyana and Jan Ravnik in fourth, and Connor and Rylee Arnold in third.

First, contestants competed in the judges’ choice round, as each judge selected a dance style for one of the contestants to perform. Second was the instant dance challenge, which tasked them to perform a number without knowing the dance style or the song until only minutes before performing it live.

The final performance was the beloved freestyle round, where all rules are out the window, leaving contestants with one final dance to wow the judges and fans.

During the judges’ choice, three couples tied for the top of the leaderboard, earning perfect scores. Those duos were Amber and Pasha; Maura and Mark; and Ezra and Daniella. Connor and Tatyana trailed closely behind, respectively scoring a 28/30 and 27/30 each.

Amber, Maura and Ezra all earned perfect scores during the instant dance round, keeping the competition neck-and-neck. Tatyana matched her first-round score with a 27/30 for her instant jive; Connor received a 25/30 for his instant cha cha.

After Tatyana and Jan performed their freestyle, a medley of “Minnie the Moocher” by Cab Calloway and “Over the Rainbow” by Judy Garland, the duo was both tearful. A piece of the professional dancer’s comments after the dance were cut out due to him saying an explicit (“She fucking killed it!” Jan reportedly said). They scored a 28/30 for their last dance of DWTS season 35.

Amber and Pasha’s freestyle was set to Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” and “Music,” a tribute to her figure skating routine performed at the 2026 Olympics. She earned a perfect score, while also dancing alongside fellow Team USA members Madison Chock and Evan Bates.

Connor and Rylee referenced Tom Holland’s iconic performance on Lip Sync Battle, set to “Singin’ in the Rain” by Gene Kelly and “Umbrella” by Rihanna. Connor even wore a recreation of Spider-Man actor’s outfit in the number equipped with fake rain on the ballroom floor, earning them a 29/30.

Maura and Mark’s final number was another high spot, earning them a 30/30 for their glamorous performance to Marilyn Monroe’s “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend,” and “The Parting Glass” and “Flowers of the Red Hill.”

Ezra and Daniella performed a touching freestyle set to “Numb” by Linkin Park. Ezra began the number without his prosthetic on, and after putting it back on, it suddenly slipped off him mid-dance. The duo recovered swiftly, though, and were joined by wheelchair dancers, and finished the dance with another prosthetic in hand, paying tribute to the amputee’s wider journey. They scored a 30/30.

Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough serve as co-hosts while Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli judge.

Also during the finale, season 34 champion Robert Irwin was on hand to announce the renewal of Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro, which will feature a cast of prospective male pro dancers who will compete for a chance to join the season 36 cast. Robert also revealed that the men will dance with fans throughout the competition, teaching them how to dance.

Alfonso and Julianne further revealed that Jackson Olson, Taylor Hanson, Tyler Cameron and all five finalists and their pros would be joining the DWTS tour in select cities. In more news, the co-hosts also announced 86 million votes had been cast in the finale alone.

For the first time, the DWTS finale aired live coast-to-coast, allowing fans in any time zone in the U.S., its territories and Canada to vote for the season 35 winner. (The show typically only airs live for the East coast, with voting taking place only during the East Coast airing of each show, leaving West Coast and Mountain time viewers unable to vote live.)

The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is typically eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode; the winner is determined by combining the judges’ scores and viewer votes in the finale episode.

Each viewer is allowed up to 10 votes per couple, per voting method (via ABC’s website and by text). Live voting takes place during the live airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance.

#646. Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders

Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

The University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

"There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum said.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

"These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet."

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases

Before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several important questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

Despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery

For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum said.

McCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

"It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he said. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early."

A great value USB-powered projector that fits in your pocket, offering sharp but static space-themed images. It’s an ideal small gift for stargazers of all ages — just make sure you buy the right model and don’t believe the misleading AI adverts.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

It was only a matter of time, but AI has come for astronomy accessories. I’ve yet to see a fictional elderly craftsman begging you to buy his hand-carved telescopes; however, it has absolutely muddied the waters around this viral gooseneck Galaxy Projector Night Light.

The good news is that there is an impressive little star projector to be had here, and I’m here to cut through the AI-assisted hype. To make sure you’re not hoodwinked, I’ve done the online legwork to bring you the best version of this device, and it won’t cost you a fortune to put a planetarium in your pocket.

Before we dive into what makes this Galaxy Projector Night Light so great, there are a couple of pressing issues to address. No variant of this USB-powered star projector will break up heated dinner arguments by casting a beautifully animated space whale on the ceiling, as one ridiculous AI-generated advert asserts. Its projections are eye-catching enough to entertain space fans young and old, but they’re strictly static.

Also, while you might be tempted by the lure of 24 interchangeable slides, compared to this Galaxy Projector Night Light’s 13, this lesser model’s slide selection is a letdown. Not only are the slides smaller and blurrier than this model, a large number are dedicated to seasonal holidays. As much as I enjoy Christmas, if I had Santa’s colossal face gazing down at me from the ceiling I’d never sleep again.

I tempered my expectations when I first got my hands on the Galaxy Projector Night Light. Packed in a small, relatively unassuming box, it looks remarkably similar to the standard model that’s spread across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and so on. Just like that one, it’s powered via USB, with a flexible stalk, a slot for slides and a nose-mounted focus wheel.

However, once I hooked it up to a handy USB socket, all my reservations vanished, and I was seriously impressed by the power of this little projector. You’ll need a darkened room but the Galaxy Projector Night Light’s larger lens is a serious step-up from the run-of-the-mill version. Its images are richer and clearer than you’d expect from a projector this size, and easily capable of transforming a mid-sized ceiling or wall into a cosmic display.

This stunning James Webb Space Telescope image of the Pillars of Creation, with its vast columns of gas and dust, is a perfect example of the projections on offer. The fact the display was static didn’t diminish its wow factor, and I spent a good 15 minutes gazing at it in wonder.

The Galaxy Projector Night Light does have a four-hour shut-off in case you drift off or want to use it to lull a child to sleep (and 12 hours for its night light function). It’s easy to adjust thanks to its flexible neck, and while it never once came loose, you’ll find some USB ports have a tighter grip than others.

Once I set aside the images of Santa Claus (you’re staying in the box, Saint Nick), jellyfish and a T. rex, I was left with 10 astronomy-related slides. Several, such as the black hole, are artistic illustrations, while others, like the aforementioned Pillars, are actual astronomical images.

They all have their own distinct appeal. I wouldn’t, for example, describe the black hole slide as relaxing, but it’s absolutely captivating in a cosmic horror way. I’d have appreciated an auto-rotate option, but that would have added some bulk to the projector.

Switching slides is a breeze, each image mounted in its own slide holder. Oddly, a couple of mine had hair-like marks, but those disappeared when I brought the image into focus via the nose wheel.

• Angel and stars (B&W)• Black hole• Earth and moon• Jellyfish• Magellanic Cloud• Milky Way• Moon and stars (B&W)• Pillars of Creation• Santa• Solar system• Starfield (B&W)• T. rex• Whale and stars (B&W)

It’s mildly disappointing that there aren’t extra slide packs out there, but the selection is ample for entertainment, relaxation and even education. What better way to spark an interest in STEM than with the wonders of space?

The Galaxy Projector Night Light will run off any USB port: a laptop, desktop, charger and so on. I even got it working with my TV’s USB socket, but the real bonus was realizing I could run it off the best power banks. If you’re on the move, slip the projector and slides into one pocket, a powerbank into another, and you’re good to go for hours.

Some of the best star projectors are styled so they blend in with a room, but this one is so small you can just pack it away until you need it. The projector’s marketing even advertises it for use in the car, which seems like an accident waiting to happen. Only the Blisslights Starport is smaller, but then you’re limited to laser-dot stars.

There’s no remote and no sound options, but the Galaxy Projector Night Light is so easy to use that children should be able to get to grips with it. Literally, in fact, since while the light portion warms up, it never really gets hot. Factor in its small size and pocket-friendly price, and it’s an ideal space gift or stocking stuffer for a young stargazer.

As long as you don’t buy the hype and think you’re getting something that’ll bathe a room in beautifully animated starscapes, as several Amazon purchasers did, you’ll find this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a surprisingly capable little star projector.

Are there bigger and better models out there? Yes, and we’ve rounded up the best star projectors if this one isn’t for you. But for convenience, value for money and portability, this Galaxy Projector Night Light is a great way to bring the cosmos into your home and it’s fast cemented itself as one of my favorites.

#644. ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ to Dominate Thanksgiving Box Office as ‘Focker In-Law,’ ‘Hexed’ Join Fray

'Hershey' and 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' also head to the big screen for the five-day holiday weekend.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to continue feasting at the box office as Focker In-Law and Hexed join the festivities over the Thanksgiving weekend.

After opening in first place last weekend with $119 million domestically and a global haul of $225 million, Lionsgate’s sixth film in the Hunger Games franchise is expected to continue its reign atop the box office. Playing in 4,018 North American theaters, Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to earn north of $60 million and could hit upwards of $80 million and beyond. The $150 million-budgeted film hopes to build on solid word of mouth, earning an A- CinemaScore and holding a 94 score from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, along with a 68 from critics. Related Stories Movies Francis Lawrence Signed On for One 'Hunger Games' Movie. Five Films Later, He's the Keeper of Panem Movies 'Hexed' Review: Hailee Steinfeld and Rashida Jones Lead a Disney Fantasy More Enchanting in Its Spectacle Than Its Storytelling

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is already off to a killer start this week, notching the highest-grossing opening Monday domestically in the history of the franchise that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games. Sunrise on the Reaping collected $12.8 million on Monday, topping the $12.3 million for 2013’s Catching Fire. Over the weekend, Sunrise debuted with the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history, which also ranked No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. Its $56 million domestic sum on Friday gave the new prequel film the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, behind Catching Fire and The Hunger Games.

“I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call,” Lionsgate film chief Adam Fogelson told The Hollywood Reporter in a recent conversation about his hopes to work with author Suzanne Collins on bringing the franchise back to the big screen. Joseph Zada stars in the new movie as Haymitch Abernathy, whom Woody Harrelson portrayed for the first four titles.

Disney releases animated offering Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the studio projecting a five-day opening around $45 million. Directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand’s movie, which carries a hefty budget north of $200 million, is expected to draw females and families, with the coming weeks clear of new animated competition until Paramount’s Angry Birds 3 in a month.

The studio feels optimistic about opening an original animated property following the bows for Sony’s Goat and Pixar’s Hoppers. But there have also been recent ones to have struggled, such as DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island, while Laika’s Wildwood has faced a formidable path to profitability, given its budget.

Hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster lead the voice cast for Hexed, which centers on a mother and her teenage daughter grappling with the girl’s magical powers. The film holds a 66 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes, with critic Angie Han writing in her review for THR that Hexed offers “more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.”

Universal Pictures revives its Meet the Parents franchise with Focker In-Law, marking the fourth feature in the series that kicked off with the original 2000 release. As the series’ first installment in 16 years, Focker In-Law launches in more than 3,350 North American locations on Wednesday, with the studio projecting around $45 million for the five-day frame. Universal split the $90 million budget with Paramount Pictures — which co-produces and handles international distribution — as the film is projected to collect an additional $30 million from 62 international territories. Given the challenges for theatrical comedies in recent years, the budget — down from the reported $100 million for the most recent franchise entry, 2010’s Little Fockers — could present a high bar for profitability.

John Hamburg, a franchise vet who worked on the scripts for all three previous features — including 2004’s Meet the Fockers and 2010’s Little Fockers — takes over in the director’s chair. He follows Jay Roach, who helmed the first two titles, and Chris Weitz, who directed Little Fockers. Meet the Parents opened to $28.6 million domestically in 2000 (en route to its $166.2 million domestic cume), with Meet the Fockers launching even bigger with $46.1 million ($279.1 million domestic cume). Little Fockers slipped a bit with its $30.8 million opening ($148.4 million domestic cume).

Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro reprise their franchise roles alongside newcomer Ariana Grande, with all three stars being central to the global marketing. Grande, who becomes a Thanksgiving mainstay after dominating the frame for the past two years with the Wicked features, plays the potential daughter-in-law to Greg Focker (Stiller) as she gets to know their family. Critics haven’t needed a lie detector test to share their honest opinions on the latest sequel that holds a challenging 28 percent critical score from Rotten Tomatoes, far below the original’s 85 score but thankfully above Little Fockers’ painful 10 rating.

In his review for THR, critic Frank Scheck wrote that Focker In-Law “feels like the nadir in a series that recycles the same tired jokes in increasingly desperate manner.”

Also hoping to whet appetites at the multiplex over the holiday frame are Angel Studios’ biographical Hershey, starring Finn Wittrock as chocolate pioneer Milton S. Hershey and Alexandra Daddario as wife Catherine. Director Mark Waters’ movie launches in 2,275 theaters, with Scheck calling it “a blandly sanitized biopic that’s as sickly sweet as the candies the company sells.”

Debuting exclusively in Imax is Netflix’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which sees Brad Pitt reprise the titular role he originated in Sony’s 2019 hit Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. After helming the original film, Quentin Tarantino penned the script for the follow-up that David Fincher stepped in to direct.

Set to begin streaming Dec. 23, the new movie hits 550 Imax screens worldwide and focuses on Pitt’s stuntman and fixer navigating Hollywood in the late 1970s. THR chief film critic David Rooney deemed it “sexy, seductive and chaotic in mostly fun ways.”

#643. ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Finalist Connor Wood Has Already Won: “I Feel Really Good”

The 31-year-old comedian has made it to the finale of the dance competition series show, even though he never quite expected it: "I really can't put my finger on why this clicked for me, but I leaned in a lot."

Comedian and podcaster Connor Wood has become a bit of a fan favorite on this season of Dancing With the Stars. “If we’re not in practice, I feel like I’m missing practice,” the 31-year-old tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom call. It’s a rare rainy day in Los Angeles, and the season 35 contestant is finding a second to rest amidst crazy rehearsal schedules.

He and partner Rylee Arnold have taken each challenge in stride. The pair have found themselves amongst the five couples advancing to the show’s finale, airing Tuesday night. Wood’s viral social media moments have certainly helped endear viewers, however, his steadily improving dancing skills don’t hurt. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Season 35 Couples Perform Their Last Dances as a Winner Is Crowned in the Finale: See the Scores, Who Won (Updating Live) TV Where to Stream 'Dancing With the Stars' Season 35 Finale Live Online

“I have been really intentional about my life and making sure I don’t ever work really hard,” he says, cheekily. “This has changed that completely, flipped it on its head.”

Heading into the final episode, he and the dancers are working with six hours a day of rehearsal to get themselves in prime condition. “Every minute of that is necessary for the show,” he notes.

Below, Wood speaks with THR about heading into the DWTS finale, the reaction to his viral Jennifer Lawrence moment and dealing with the online hate.

I feel really good. Me and Rylee, we went into the semifinals, and that was the hard part. It was two brand new dances, two long dances, two very fast hard dances, and this one is fun. We’re going out there, we’re putting on a show. It really is for us, which is fun. It’s for the fans, [but] it’s [also] for us. It’s something that hasn’t been seen before. We’re doing a really cool dichotomy of dances too.

The day after the show, we film basically what you see before we dance. We do all of the face-to-face interviews. We do the one-on-one interview, and then we do the group session interview. This is obviously a bigger one. There’s three dances, so they have three videos that they had to make. There’s one for each dance, and then they’ll film rehearsal and stuff for the filler. But I also have the podcast that I do, so that was 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., and then we filmed from 12 p.m to 10 p.m.

It was long, but it’s all needed. That’s the thing. Sometimes you go onto a set or something, and it’s like we’re doing a take for the 15th time, and I’m like, “I promise you I’m getting worse. Every time we do another one, I promise you’re getting a worse take from me.” This is not the case. This one you do get better as you put more hours in, which is an annoying, frustrating thing that that is true. The harder you work, the better you get.

What were you expecting for yourself coming in versus where you are now?

I wasn’t expecting anything for myself, honestly. I’ve only ever danced at weddings. I have no pride when it comes to sticking with something. I’m happy to throw in the towel. You’ll quit while you’re ahead. I’ll quit while I’m behind. I don’t think there’s any shame in that. I am competitive though, which is weird. We had to stop playing Monopoly in my family home because I took it too seriously. But that wasn’t part of this — I really can’t put my finger on why this clicked for me, but I leaned in a lot. I’ve done some really TikTok cringe things that I wouldn’t normally have done. It’s been so well received, it’s a vulnerability thing, I guess, that’s been nice to be a part of.

How do you get through these red carpets to make it an actually enjoyable experience?

That’s my bread and butter. Hamming it up on the carpet with interviews, that is my Dancing With The Stars. A funny thing that I’ve realized is that obviously I’m not the best dancer on the show or even freaking close. I’m aware of that. I feel like people don’t realize that. I don’t think I’m Zeus on the dance floor. I’m very aware of what I’m capable of, but people also aren’t seeing that dance is a part of the whole of this show, and doing press and meeting fans and doing X, Y, Z, it all makes up that whole. Anytime we spend these 12, 15 hour days creating packages and personifying these people that are on TV, it helps the case. If they see that you’re working really hard, if they see that you’re having fun in the press lines. If you’re being vulnerable, and you’re oversharing, people really like that, they relate to it. That’s what that is. I look forward to doing interviews because that’s where I feel like I hit my stride on the dance floor is after the dance, and I can talk about how hard it was to learn in Argentine Tango.

Do you feel more confident in dancing now?

Yes, and I that’s a natural progression with this whole thing. I’m learning the dances faster because I’ve been learning dance for three months. There’s a baseline or a foundation that I’m pulling from. When Rylee gives me “Start here” and “do this,” I know what she’s talking about. I realized recently I’m personifying each dance. When a dance was really hard, I began to resent the dance on day two of rehearsal because I’m like, “We are not getting along, me and the samba, we’re not getting along. I don’t get the samba. It doesn’t make sense to me.” Getting past those couple weeks — I hit my stride in probably week six in this competition because I was not resenting the dance. It became easier for me to learn the dances. We saw my dancing. It’s not the best, but I am having a lot more fun because I’m enjoying the process way more.

With the show and being online, do you feel a bit of an overload? I’m sure you’re not looking forward to hearing “8th Avenue” or “smoothie” said to you ever again. (Laughs).

I like when everybody’s on board with something. What a harmless thing for everyone to be having fun with. That’s good, clean, fun. It’s easy. I know a lot of marketing coordinators probably had a really great weekly meeting when they turned in their social media reports and they had a video with a million views on their page for brand X, Y, Z, football team X, Y, Z. Everyone had so much fun. Everyone got to put a spin on that. That fired me up.

The rest of the internet, totally different story right now. We’ve gotten to a point where I have become a bit of a villain for some people.

I think that they think that I personally voted their favorite off, and it’s like — I’m aware of my level of dance skill. I have nothing to do with me staying here. That’s just been just the dark side of making it as far as we made it. My understanding is that the more that people go home, the more the fans of those people will go to someone else’s page and villainize those people. That’s sad, and it’s just a testament to how invested people are in this show. A cool part of this show is that the fans are so invested. Like I said, the 8th Avenue thing, it’s fun for people to be a part of things. Being on the other side of that is not as fun. It’s part of the game. I signed up for it. I’ve never experienced that.

It has to be tough given social media is a huge part of your job. You can’t disengage as much.

Yeah. As we’ve gone through the season… First of all, I’m like, “Well, not getting on Twitter the rest of the season. That’s a really interesting group of people.” You want to get home from the 15-hour day, and you want to lay on your couch, your Lola blanket swaddling you like a newborn. Turn off your brain, look at your phone. The first thing on your phone is, “Connor Wood’s still here? Who’s he paying at ABC?” OK, scroll to the next thing. But that is part of it. This is weird and sick in the head, [but] I am going to miss every part of this experience. If you have haters — you’ve been around long enough to have a hater — that means you’re doing something really, really well. I’ve been lucky enough. I will say, I’m not cut out for public scrutiny. This is not something for me. This will be my last reality show.

I mean, [if] they come knocking — Of course, I’ll open the door. But at least for Traitors, they’re going to take my phone. No, but it’s great. I’ve been lucky enough to make it this far, and it’s just part of the competition. We got a couple days left.

#642. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale."

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth."

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons."

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data."

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to important advances in understanding nature.

"This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success."

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

SpaceX set a new record with its latest satellite launch out of California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Launch Complex-4E on Sunday (Nov. 22) at 7:23 a.m. ET (1223 GMT; 4:23 a.m. local time in California), on a mission for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) called NROL-136.

It was the second launch from that pad in a little over 32 hours, after the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force. And that quick turnaround made history.

Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn! 🏎️🚀🏎️🚀November 22, 2026

"Massive high five to the @SpaceX west coast team for a world record launch to launch turn from Pad 4e last night! 32 hr, 3 min, 21 sec! This smashed the previous record of 45 hrs from Pad 40. Team got there with several hours of margin. Next goal… the 24 hr turn!" Kiko Dontchev, SpaceX's vice president of launch, said via X on Sunday. (Pad 40 is at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.)

NROL-136 was the sixth launch of 2026 so far for the NRO. All of them have been carried out by SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, and all have delivered classified satellites to low Earth orbit.

The launch marked another step in the NRO's effort to expand its intelligence-gathering capabilities through a proliferated network of spacecraft designed to provide more frequent and timely surveillance of locations around the globe.

About two minutes after liftoff, the Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued carrying the classified payloads onward to orbit. The booster then reversed course and returned to Vandenberg, touching down at Landing Zone 4 approximately seven and a half minutes after launch.

Saturday's launch was the 14th flight for this particular Falcon 9 booster, dubbed B1097, which previously launched NASA's Sentinel-6B ocean-monitoring satellite, NROL-172, USSF-259 for the Space Force, and eight Starlink missions.

NROL-136 was the 15th launch dedicated to building the NRO's "proliferated architecture," the satellites for which have been developed in partnership with SpaceX and Northrop Grumman. The network is designed to increase coverage and improve the "capability and resilience" of U.S. intelligence operations in space, according to the NRO's mission website.

The NRO began deploying the constellation in May 2024 with the launch of NROL-146. The most recent proliferated architecture mission before Sunday was NROL-179, which lifted off on June 19, 2026.

As with any classified mission, the agency has not disclosed the exact number of satellites aboard NROL-136 or revealed details about their onboard technologies.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 11 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 with the news that NROL-136 set a new record for the shortest time between two launches from the same pad.

#639. A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, new research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," said Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the new paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely."

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution

The conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

At first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

The problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations

Another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Important genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are quickly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst said: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'."

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory

To investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date."

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more important for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

If the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst said: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate."

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more important genes receive special protection.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate."

That does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Professor Hurst said: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm."

The research therefore provides new support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most important genes by reducing how often they mutate.

Materials provided by University of Bath. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#638. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.

Amazon's first satellite launch since a rocket failure that doomed 40 of its spacecraft went off without a hitch Tuesday morning (Nov. 24).

An Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation lifted off at 6:14 a.m. EST (1114 GMT) from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, on Tuesday (Nov. 23), right at the end of the 29-minute window that opened at 6:45 a.m. EST (1045 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time in Kourou).

The launch was originally supposed to take place on Monday (Nov. 23), but that attempt was scrubbed due to a technical issue affecting the rocket's ground support systems, according to Arianespace.

Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit, will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.

Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur, suffered a problem shortly after launch.

Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's New Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9.

Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And New Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test.

The Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure.

This morning's launch was the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year.

He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #635. Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. New research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

The study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

Members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

These contrasting perspectives may have important consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science

Dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

Some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as new challenges arise.

Dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

One possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

The differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when new evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

With researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

The study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

"Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she says. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind."

Materials provided by Santa Fe Institute. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
