The Shenzhou-24 mission lifted off today (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. ET.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program.

A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25).

You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV).

Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong, a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022.

Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023.)

China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025, with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training.

We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch.

This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest.

Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu.

Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24.

According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

#578. A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

New research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow new stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, said the research provides new insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

"At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis said.

"In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed."

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way

The Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

As the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

Studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis said.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated."

Observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

However, the new findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

"We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she said.

The possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

New Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

"Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis said.

The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

"By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis said.

The authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

#577. Germany's 2027 budget: A record €561 billion and a mountain of debt

The 2027 federal budget proposal has finally been hammered out and is set for a vote in parliament. What are the government's policy priorities in defense, infrastructure, the economy and social spending?

It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

Following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government plans to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

But here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the new debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

This development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

To understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social issues, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding new investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

What's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary."

The rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are plans for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

The pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

The Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

At the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

This would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an important point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

At the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.

The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos.

The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system.

Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth.

For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth.

But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid, meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet.

Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

#574. A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

Some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

Researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

If the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

The interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

"There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb says. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into."

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of New York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Big Bang

Not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

Heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

These extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

To investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star

The researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

The situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

In this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

The process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb says.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within

Once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

The team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

Over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how quickly the star rotates.

If the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

"Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb says. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time."

As the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

"This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done."

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

Their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

"We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb says. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard."

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

However, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

Astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

"For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb says. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations."

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

For now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the new research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

Coming complete with a smartphone app, the YunLone Galaxy Projector can project just about any color combination you can think of onto the ceiling. It has a built-in Bluetooth speaker, too, offering all-around relaxation and an ambience setting.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector is an inexpensive but effective way to bring the marvel of space into your living room or bedroom. Costing around $28, this star projector can display beautiful dancing auroras across your walls and ceiling, and thanks to app support, a huge range of color options are available. In fact, the color combinations you can display here are almost infinite.

With built-in sounds, a Bluetooth speaker and endless customization options, this really is an all-singing, all-dancing star projector. We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic.

This isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector. But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light. You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however.

That isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. Given the wide reach of the projector, it helps spread the aurora lights across your entire room.

The projector has a solid build quality: It's plastic but feels sturdy and well-made. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. Those rubber feet help prevent it from being knocked off a desk or bedside table, too.

As already mentioned, the YunLone Galaxy Projector isn't a scientific star projector. If you want to recreate actual constellations and close-ups of planets on your bedroom ceiling, this is not the projector for you. But if you're looking for beautiful, mesmerizing aurora-style patterns, it's a great choice.

Once you're connected to the app, you can control exactly what colors the projector displays. Not only can you choose from a number of preset arrangements — labeled as seasons, colors or holidays, so you can create a mood that matches the time of year or how you feel — but you can set your own entire color scheme by choosing from a color wheel. You can also set the brightness, whether the lights will have a "breathing" effect, and how fast they ripple across your ceiling.

It's a very neat touch, and it goes beyond what we'd expect to find in a star projector in this price range. If you don't want to bother with app connection, you can still set a range of colors and options from the remote control, but the options here are more limited.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector comes equipped with a laser, so it can project green laser stars onto your walls and ceiling. We didn't love the look of these, though, so it's good that you can turn them off independently of the aurora lights. You can also change the laser's brightness if you'd like the stars to appear dimmer.

Both the laser stars and the aurora projections have a very wide reach, covering most of the walls and ceiling of the bedroom we tested the unit in. Obviously, this will vary depending on the size of your room and how far away from the ceiling/wall you place the unit, but we were pleasantly surprised by the coverage offered by this projector.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector has a companion app that can be downloaded onto an Android or Apple smartphone. Once the app is set up and paired with your unit, you have full control over the colors, speed and brightness of your projections.

The pairing process isn't entirely straightforward, however, with no simple way of forcing the projector to enter pairing mode. The instructions tell you to quickly turn the unit on and off three times, but it took several attempts before we successfully put the projector into pairing mode.

Thankfully, once that's done, it should stay paired with your smartphone permanently so you won't have to repeat the process. And the app itself is very easy to use, working seamlessly to change the colors of the projection unit.

The bundled remote control (which requires two AAA batteries, not included) is a little more complex than most, offering a range of buttons to control both the built-in speaker and the light itself. We'd highly recommend opting for the app option as it gives you much better control over the unit, but if your smartphone is unavailable, you can at least set basic color and speed with the remote.

You can connect a music player to the projector via Bluetooth to play your own audio through its built-in speaker. The quality is decent rather than outstanding: It obviously doesn't match the sound of a specialist speaker, but it's as good as we'd expect any $28 speaker to be. It lacks the bass that music requires to sound "complete" but will be ideal for listening to audiobooks and podcasts.

In a neat touch, the YunLone Galaxy Projector also has eight built-in sound effects, including white noise, waves, lullabies and a storm, which some users may find relaxing and good to fall asleep to.

We have been thoroughly impressed with what the YunLone Galaxy Projector offers. Its projections are beautiful auroras that dance across your ceiling, and the ability to fully customize the color and speed is something that we really didn't expect to find at a $28 price point.

If you're on a budget and looking for a non-scientific projector to use to relax and unwind with, we really don't think you can find a better unit. If, however, you want something that offers more scientific projections, you'll need to look elsewhere.

Sega Toys' range of projectors, including the Homestar Flux and the Homestar Classic, is excellent but comes with a much bigger price tag. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector is worth considering too, offering realistic projections but with a price tag closer to $50.

The good thing about these projectors is that they come with interchangeable discs, able to display various images of space. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector has several discs in the box, but you'll need to buy extra discs for the Sega Toys range, so that’s an extra cost to factor in.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

#571. Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

Researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering new clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the new evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

The discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious New Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection

At the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

"What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," said Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future."

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences

To uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

Rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

The databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

"The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically."

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions

Beyond identifying the new viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past."

New AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries

The research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

"If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque said. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts."

"We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper.

New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity.

As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf, the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived "red giant" phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris.

During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space.

To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming.

"Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action."

The team was able to determine that this gas shell of IRAS 06530-0213 is around half a light-year wide and was ejected into space around 6,500 years ago. It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life.

The team thinks that for around 2,000 years after the pulse, the star lost mass at a lower rate. This mass loss then increased sharply over the following 1,000 years. This led to the creation of a lumpy shell of gas now seen as a tangle of material filaments around the dying star. The fact that these filaments have a spiral shape could indicate that IRAS 06530-0213 has an unseen partner orbiting it, stirring the gas.

Meanwhile, the hourglass-shaped nebula immediately around the star began to take shape around 700 years ago, meaning that the red giant phase for IRAS 06530-0213 only ended very recently, in cosmic terms at least.

There are also unexpected elements to the ALMA observations of IRAS 06530-0213.

The team discovered an unexpected abundance of heavy versions, or isotopes, of elements like carbon, oxygen and nitrogen around IRAS 06530-0213.

This doesn't conform to models of how stars like IRAS 06530-0213 forge elements and mix them into their surroundings, though similar signatures have been seen around odd stellar objects, with violent bursts of nuclear fusion thought to be the cause.As well as seeing something unexpected, the researchers didn't detect something they expected to observe.

Dying stars like IRAS 06530-0213 have previously been known to have companions, typically sitting with them inside compact disks of dust. These disks are indirect evidence of material being dragged from the close companion star to the dying star. This is a process scientists have used to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.

However, ALMA failed to detect such disk around IRAS 06530. The team suggests that this could be because a disk existed, albeit briefly, during which time it powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass, following this the disk simply faded away.

"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai concluded. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."The team's research was published on Friday (Nov. 20) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #568. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists aren't convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

#567. NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar

A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It’s one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us.

With its graceful spiral arms and central bar of stars, NGC 4394 closely resembles what astronomers think our home galaxy, the Milky Way, would look like if we were able to view it from a similar face-on vantage point. In a universe full of arcing spiral galaxies and nebulae organically shaped by the death and birth of stars, straight streaks of stars like NGC 4394’s galactic bar stand out. Galactic bars are extremely common; astronomers estimate 65 percent of nearby spiral galaxies have one. Hubble has imaged a wide variety of stunning barred spiral galaxies, including NGC 5728, NGC 685, and NGC 613, but how do these striking features form?

Explanations for how galactic bars might form tend to center on a galaxy’s disk of stars becoming unstable. This could happen because of gravitational nudges from passing galaxies, interactions between stars, or other forces. Once the disk becomes unstable, the circular orbits of stars become elongated, leading to the barred shape seen in galaxies like NGC 4394. Observations show that galactic bars are more common among galaxies in the universe today than they were several billion years ago. Though stellar bars are in fashion today, research suggests that this is only temporary; as bars become more massive, they can themselves become unstable.

In addition to their stellar bars and spiral arms, NGC 4394 and the Milky Way galaxy share another important similarity, in that they might both contain a LINER (low-ionization nuclear emission-line region). LINER refers to an area near the center of a galaxy where its spectra feature certain ionized or neutral elements. Researchers do not yet know exactly how LINERs form, though either hungry supermassive black holes or intense star formation likely play a role.

Hubble has paid a visit to NGC 4394’s patch of sky more than once, and a previous image of NGC 4394 was released a decade ago. That image was part of an observing program (#10515; PI: Peng) that focused on NGC 4394’s galactic neighbor, Messier 85. While one of Hubble’s instruments examined Messier 85 to study its unusual collection of star clusters, another (Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys) captured a parallel area of the sky that contained NGC 4394.

Today’s image also incorporates observations from a recent program (#18103; PI: Thilker) dedicated to understanding how star formation comes to an end in galaxies in dense cluster environments, and how this process differs from more isolated galaxies adrift in the field. For this observing program, researchers used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 and its sensitivity to a broad wavelength range to determine the ages of individual star clusters. NGC 4394 is one of 40 galaxies they studied in this way.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov

#566. Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

New archaeological research from Bournemouth University (BU) suggests that an influential Iron Age British ruler, long believed to have been a man, was actually a woman. The ruler, known as Verica, played a pivotal role in events leading to the Roman invasion of Britain in AD 43. The findings challenge longstanding assumptions about early British history and the political influence of women during this period.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, a powerful tribe whose lands extended across much of what is now Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and escaped to Rome, where the exiled ruler sought assistance from Emperor Claudius.

The Roman historian Cassius Dio claimed that Verica's appeal was the reason Claudius decided to invade Britain. If this account is accurate, Verica's actions may have helped set in motion one of the most consequential events in British history.

Ancient Evidence Challenges an Iron Age King's Identity

Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, led the research and argues that earlier historians incorrectly identified Verica as male.

"Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female."

Russell points to several pieces of evidence supporting this interpretation. One is the name Verica itself, which ends in the letter "a," a feature common among female names of the time. Other prominent examples include Cartimandua, who ruled the Brigantes (in Yorkshire), and Boudica, leader of the Iceni (in Norfolk).

All three rulers lived during roughly the same period. Boudica is the best known because of her rebellion against Roman rule in AD 60. However, Russell argues that Verica may have held even greater political power and influence.

Another important clue comes from coins issued under Verica's rule. These coins bear the Latin title "rex," traditionally translated as "king," which has contributed to the assumption that Verica was male. Russell explains that the title was not necessarily restricted to men.

"People also assume she was a 'he' because of the term 'rex' on coins, but rex is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous."

He continued: "The use of the Latin title rex on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor."

The artwork on Verica's coins provides another intriguing clue. Rather than depicting the masculine warriors commonly featured on coins produced by other British Iron Age rulers, Verica's coins show a figure with distinctly feminine characteristics.

"Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback."

The Forgotten Ruler Behind Rome's Invasion of Britain

Russell believes Verica's importance extended far beyond the ruler's identity. He argues that Verica may have been instrumental in helping Claudius successfully invade Britain.

Ancient Roman writers frequently portrayed Claudius as an ineffective emperor who was easily influenced by women and formerly enslaved people who had gained their freedom. This reputation may have shaped how historians described Verica's role in persuading him to invade.

Russell suggests that Cassius Dio's account reinforced this negative portrayal by presenting the invasion as a decision made under the influence of a woman. In reality, he argues, Verica may have been a valuable political and military ally who supplied the Romans with intelligence and practical assistance.

"The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked. In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica's role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her on board ensured the project was a success, as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.

"The invasion was Claudius' great triumph -- it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it."

For Claudius, the conquest of Britain offered an opportunity to establish his reputation as a successful military commander. Verica's removal from power gave him a political justification for intervening, while the exiled ruler's knowledge of Britain may have helped the Roman forces achieve their objectives.

Could Rome's Conquest of Britain Have Been Avoided?

Although Verica was an important political figure in late Iron Age Britain, the ruler's influence has received relatively little attention compared with that of other prominent leaders.

Russell believes the archaeological evidence supports recognizing Verica as one of Britain's earliest and most significant female rulers. He also raises the possibility that the Roman invasion might never have occurred without Verica's exile and subsequent appeal to Claudius.

"We should take the archaeological evidence at face value" says Russell "and remember Verica as a female-king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed, fleeing to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place."

New Insights Into Women in Iron Age Britain

The findings build on earlier Bournemouth University research exploring the position of women in ancient British society.

Last year, a study involving Russell and other BU researchers uncovered evidence of a matriarchal society in Iron Age Britain. The research indicated that husbands moved into their wives' communities after marriage, suggesting that women occupied a central position in the social structure.

Together, these discoveries are prompting researchers to reconsider the influence women may have exercised in Iron Age Britain, both within their communities and in the political decisions that shaped the region's future.

Russell's research on Verica is presented in the new book Caratacus: Great king of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902). The findings are also discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

#565. Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO: Trump, Musk, Altman react while the internet has jokes

Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he stepped down, and less than a week after the company's board said it had no intention of bringing him back. Reactions to Huang's return have been a mix of praise, criticism, and jokes, with several other tech executives rallying around him.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Nov. 12, a day after the board accepted it with immediate effect. He stepped down amid reports that he'd had extramarital affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and a Nvidia employee, with allegations of a third affair with another worker subsequently surfacing. His relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) drew particular scrutiny, as she was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips. She previously worked as an executive at Megaspeed, a company U.S. authorities have been investigating over concerns it smuggled advanced Nvidia chips to China in circumvention of U.S. restrictions.

While Huang said that he would be "honored" to return as CEO if asked, the board said on Nov. 17 that it did not plan to bring him back. Yet after reported pressure from President Donald Trump, the chipmaker has put Huang back in the top job after all. In a press release announcing Huang's reinstatement, Nvidia stated that it had based the decision on "input from senior levels of the United States government."

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," said Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones, who last week said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen."

Trump has been characteristically celebratory about Nvidia's decision, making several posts on his social media platform Truth Social on the topic. This included an edited image based on a photo of Trump after a shooter attempted to assassinate him in 2024. Originally posted by X account @grandoldmemes, the picture has been edited to show Huang holding a red bra aloft as a Nvidia banner is displayed in the background.

Calling Huang's reinstatement an "absolutely GREAT decision" (emphasis original), Trump stated that having him installed as Nvidia's CEO is vital to the U.S. economy.

"The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy," wrote Trump. "The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security…. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure."

The U.S. president also spoke about Huang's reinstatement in a phone call to CNBC on Monday.

"I think he's gonna start off at an almost higher level," Trump said. "He's apologised for [his] indiscretion, which was unfortunate. Probably that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas. Now [CNBC host Jim] Cramer would not know that because he’s a very, very, very committed person. But sex sells."

Trump's on-and-off ally Elon Musk also celebrated Huang's return, reposting Nvidia's announcement on X and writing that "the mistake has been corrected." Last week, Musk stated that he was signing a petition to reinstate Nvidia's then-ousted CEO.

"Everyone I know at Nvidia wanted Jensen back and it shows," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO continued, sharing a post from investor Gavin Baker. In it, Baker shared images of people crowding around Huang and applauding him on his return to Nvidia's offices.

"Grateful to the President, everyone in the administration, everyone who signed the petition, everyone who supported Jensen publicly, everyone who called the board, everyone on the board who fought for him, everyone," Baker wrote. Musk himself was ousted as CEO of X.com in 2000 after it merged with Confinity, the company behind PayPal. He had reportedly wanted to phase out the PayPal name in favor of X.com, despite concerns about its explicit connotations.

Various other prominent figures in tech have also voiced support for Huang's return, several of whom have previously faced comparable turmoil at their own companies.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman appeared to express approval for Huang's reinstatement, publishing a post on X that simply read, "Jensen!" Altman went through a similar incident when OpenAI's board fired him in 2023, accusing him of lying, retaliating against critics, and creating a "toxic atmosphere." Despite these allegations, Altman was ultimately reinstated after days of outcry from supporters.

Meanwhile, Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao posted to X that he was "glad to see @JensenHuang back," resharing his previous reaction that it was "a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign." Zhao resigned from his role as CEO of Binance and pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program in 2023, serving a four-month prison sentence. However, he remains Binance's majority shareholder and retains significant influence over the global cryptocurrency exchange.

Uber co-founder and former CEO Travis Kalanick weighed in as well, stating that he would "always sign up to serve" Huang. Kalanick had previously posted support for reinstating Huang at Nvidia and asked followers to share "some great ideas for how to 'persuade' the Nvidia board to bring Jensen back."

"Jensen is a great man, flawed like the rest of us, but at the same time the best amongst us," Kalanick posted to X on Monday. "The world and humanity needs him to fight for a shot at liberty, a counterweight to techno-authoritarianism."

Kalanick resigned from his role as Uber CEO in 2017 after demands from multiple major investors. This came after Kalanick took a leave of absence amid allegations of a misogynistic workplace culture. Though one of the investors sued Kalanick for fraud later that year, the ousted CEO remained on Uber's board until resigning in 2019.

Telegram CEO Pavel Durov also celebrated Huang's return, posting "Jensen's back" with a party popper emoji. He then joked about the situation, writing that "Nvidia's board finally accepted that a CEO has to evaluate Chinese models personally. You can't delegate that."

Durov was ousted from his former role as CEO of Russian social media platform VK in 2014 after the board said it had accepted a resignation he'd submitted and failed to withdraw. Durov claimed the resignation had been an April Fools' joke and suggested that his firing was politically motivated.

Given their own personal experiences, it's no surprise that many former and current tech executives have supported Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO. Other reactions have been a mixed bag — some celebrating the news, some condemning it, and others simply enjoying the jokes and memes.

"Reinstating Huang is a disaster for corporate governance and even the rule of law, but it is objectively very very funny," author and tech reporter David Z. Morris posted to X.

Some have also noted the timing of Huang's temporary ousting, joking that he deliberately orchestrated several days away from work in order to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

It's been a tumultuous few weeks for Nvidia, and it's unclear how the company plans to move forward at this stage. However, whatever happens, the jokes will likely continue for a while.

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.
